news.title: US may stop trade with EU if Canada becomes associated member — Trump
news.text:
WASHINGTON, September 17. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump said his country may halt trade with European countries if Canada is granted the status of the EU associated member.

"If I think it’s a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters in North Carolina.

He said the response will be conditioned on the "intention" of European leaders.

"If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we will put very heavy tariffs on Europe," Trump said.

The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on September 12, citing sources, that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is considering associate membership in the European Union, which would give Ottawa a range of economic and political benefits without formally joining the bloc.

The premier commented on these reports on September, saying that his country would seek to build a "unique alliance" with the EU without formal membership. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on September 16 that the union will invite Canada to become its first associated member.
news.summary: The US president said the response will depend on whether he thinks "it’s a hostile act"
news.author: Tass

news.title: Trump lashes out at Fed after Warsh backs rate hike
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday leveled his most pointed — though still indirect — criticism ​yet at his hand-picked Federal Reserve chief, fuming on social media over the central bank’s move to raise interest rates in a bid to calm persistent inflation.

“Interest ‌Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR,” he wrote on Truth Social, his social media platform.

“LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” he concluded.

It was the closest Trump has come yet to leveling one of his broadsides directly at Kevin Warsh, though he later told reporters he still had confidence in the man he picked earlier this ​year to take over the Fed from Jerome Powell, a figure the president frequently derided for not delivering the dramatic rate cuts Trump has routinely demanded.

“I … talked to Kevin,” ​Trump said, appearing to confirm an interaction with the Fed chief that Warsh himself has so far declined to corroborate. “And I said you might ⁠as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They’re very political. They’re doing the wrong thing.”

Trump, as he has in recent social media ​posts, also appeared to connect persistent US trade deficits with the borrowing costs set by the central bank, even though the two are largely unrelated. Trump had previously threatened to cut off all ​trade from countries with which the US had trade deficits if the Fed did not cut interest rates.

“The word “Deficit” is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS. We are “carrying” almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer,” Trump posted on Wednesday.

Trump’s screed came shortly after Fed policymakers unanimously agreed on Wednesday to raise rates by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00%, an action that Warsh described at a subsequent press conference ​as “a sober decision, serious decision, responsible decision.”

“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said.

And rates are likely going still higher. New policy projections showed ​16 of 18 policymakers anticipate at least one more quarter-percentage-point hike by the end of this year, with only two of them seeing rates remaining stable from here. Warsh said again Wednesday that he is ‌opposed to sharing ⁠forward guidance and did not submit a projection.

Trump tapped Warsh in January to succeed Powell, whom Trump nicknamed “too late” for taking a more cautious approach to rate cuts last year than Trump wanted. Warsh, for his part, took office with a pledge to maintain the Fed’s independence on setting monetary policy while at the same time working in greater concert with the White House on other matters.

Since Warsh took office in June — after a Senate confirmation that was nearly derailed by a federal investigation into Powell and renovations of the Fed headquarters building — he initially steered Fed officials to ​holding rates steady, although not all policymakers agreed ​with the approach in the face of ⁠inflationary pressures. On Wednesday, he said the time had come for the central bank to take action.

“This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have improved,” he told reporters.

Asked at his press conference if he planned to meet with Trump to explain the Fed’s decision, Warsh ​demurred.

“I don’t have anything for you on discussions with the president,” he said.

Trump’s post was the second time this week he’d taken aim ​at his own appointees. ⁠After the Supreme Court struck down his attempt to regulate how states issue mail ballots, Trump wrote of the three justices he appointed:

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves.”

White House officials spent much of the week publicly pressuring the Fed to hold rates steady. One former White House official told Reuters the ⁠president’s social media ​post about the Fed was a tame response in the context of that campaign.

“The president is making clear he ​disagrees with the policy without explicitly saying Warsh is personally to blame, giving him a nickname, or threatening retaliatory action against the Fed,” said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak ​publicly. “Instead he’s redirecting his ire toward trading partners, which have little to do with the monetary policy decision.”

news.title: Ed Sheeran, Robert Kraft donate millions for Gaza aid after Macklemore's urging
news.text:
Stadium owner Robert Kraft says he and musician Ed Sheeran will donate $US2 million ($2.8 million) for aid in Gaza in response to rapper Macklemore's pledge to give his earnings from the Loop tour to Palestinian charities. 

This morning Macklemore said the US$1 million ($1.4 million) he earnt from the two shows he played on the tour would be donated to "bring the conversation back to where it belongs: to the Palestinian people who are still being killed, still living under military occupation and still fighting for their freedom".

The rapper invited Mr Kraft, who is the owner of Gillette stadium and who concluded it would "cross the line" for Macklemore to play at the upcoming concerts at his venue, to match the donation.

"Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting," Macklemore said.

"Palestinian life is no less valuable than any other life on this Earth."

A few hours later, in a statement released by the Gillette Stadium account, Mr Kraft said he already decided he would double that donation after a call by Sheeran. 

"I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people," he said.

'I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting.

"Earlier today before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid the region to fight this humanitarian crisis."

The money will go to the Palestinian Children's Relief Fund, Heal Palestine, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Medical Aid Palestine, the United Nations Relief and Works Agency and Anera.

Mr Kraft said Sheeran now planned to reach out to other venue owners and "our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges."

"In addition I'd like the people who are speaking in support of the Palestinian people to know that for decades, I have supported efforts that create opportunity for Palestinians and have brought young Palestinians and Israelis together to build businesses, create jobs and forge relationships."

It did not say which charities the money would be donated to. 

Sheeran has not yet publicly commented. 

Macklemore, Sheeran and Mr Kraft made headlines this week after Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran's tour over his pro-Palestinian comments on stage.

Sheeran said it was not his decision, but rather the promoters of the tour and Mr Kraft. 

Mr Kraft, who is Jewish, said the decision to cancel Macklemore was a result of his recent comments "and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community".

The remaining supports acts for the tour have also dropped out in support of Macklemore.

Who is Robert Kraft?

Mr Kraft is the billionaire owner of the NFL team the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts. 

The 85-year-old built his fortune in the paper and packing industry before expanding into construction and real estate. 

Mr Kraft is credited with transforming the Patriots into one of the most successful franchises in the league's history. 

In his owner biography on the team's website it says his philanthropic efforts exceed $US1 billion and that he has established a foundation combating "anti-Semitism and all forms of hate".

Mr Kraft made headlines in 2019 when he was charged with two counts of soliciting prostitution after he was allegedly captured on video engaging in sex acts with a worker at a massage parlour in Florida. 

A spokesman for Mr Kraft said: "We categorically deny that Mr Kraft engaged in any illegal activity."

He is a close friend and supporter of US President Donald Trump, who told reporters in the Oval Office that he was "very sad" to hear about the charges at the time.

"I was very surprised to see it. He's proclaimed his innocence, totally," Mr Trump said.

Nineteen months after Mr Kraft was charged, The New York Times reported Florida prosecutors dropped the case after the recordings were thrown out by the court.
news.summary: Macklemore had challenged Robert Kraft to match his donation to Palestinian charities after the billionaire stadium owner dropped him from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour.
news.author: Georgie Hewson

news.title: AARON PATRICK: Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese both have a problem with their central banks
news.text:
President Donald Trump greeted America’s first interest rate rise in three years this morning by lashing out at the world.

The US could stop trading with any country that sells more to the US than it buys, he said, as part of a complaint about the Federal Reserve’s decision to move rates up to 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent.

“Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR,” he wrote on Truth Social.

“If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year. The word ‘Deficit’ is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS. We are ‘carrying’ almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer.”

Australia runs a trade deficit with the US, thanks to the popularity of Netflix, Apple and other big American exporters, and is therefore less likely to upset the President.

More importantly for Australia and the world, the decision shows that new Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh is willing to defy political pressure. By using interest rates to control inflation, which is at 3.4 per cent in the US, he may be able to limit the financial pressures spreading around the global economy, exacerbated by the conflict in the Middle East.

“This reaffirms that the Fed is going to be focused on inflation and that is going to take a degree of volatility and uncertainty out of the markets,” says Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger Investment Management.

Despite what economists considered long-term good news, US shares fell about 0.4 per cent. That’s because higher rates lower the value of dividends in the future, making shares less valuable.

Last week the dollar was above US72¢. After the Fed’s decision, it was just under US71¢, a sign of how interest rate differences between countries influence currencies. For travellers, visiting the US just got a little more expensive.

Same problem

The two countries face similar inflation challenges. This week demonstrated that both their governments, in different ways, like to shift blame for economic pain to their central banks.

President Trump accuses the Federal Reserve of keeping rates higher than they need to be. Anthony Albanese implies the Reserve Bank of Australia is contributing to higher prices by making loans more expensive.

“We understand that Australians are under cost-of-living pressure and that includes the impact of decisions that are made by the independent Reserve Bank,” Mr Albanese told Parliament on Wednesday during question time.

What the Prime Minister did not explain is why the Reserve Bank has raised rates three times this year, a painful process designed to kill an inflation breakout. Inflation hit 3.5 per cent on an annual basis in July.

Rising prices are caused by too much money flowing around the economy, a problem exacerbated by the Albanese government’s deficits. By conflating the existence of inflation with the cure, Mr Albanese misleads Australians and undermines respect for the Reserve Bank.

His treasurer, Jim Chalmers, is part of the problem. This week, instead of blaming the Reserve Bank for inflation, he pretended government spending is helping the fight, when the opposite is true.

“It’s why we’ve got an ambitious tax reform package, which is about cutting income taxes for workers and giving first home buyers a fair go in a housing market which has locked them out for too long,” he told Parliament.

“It’s why we’re providing cost-of-living help via the tax system, via bulk billing and via higher wages and other wages as well.”

Making it worse

The best way the government can help fight inflation is to cut spending. Instead, it has made small income-tax cuts, raised doctors’ wages and subsidised home loans — while running a $31.5 billion Budget deficit this financial year. The government doesn’t set wages, except for federal public servants, of whom it has hired an extra 28 every day it has been in office. The extra money injected into the economy makes the problem worse.

At the same time, professional economists have watched, with begrudging respect, Dr Chalmers squirm his way out of responsibility for one of the highest inflation rates in the Western world. (Worse than Indonesia, China, Mexico or Italy, according to Trading Economics, a website that tracks economic data.)

“He has been at great pains to say that inflation has nothing to do with government spending, when it does,” says Richard Holden, a professor at the University of NSW. “He is constantly blaming somebody else for the predicament we’re in.”

A formidable speaker, Dr Chalmers received a few laughs in Parliament on Wednesday when he called his Coalition counterpart, Tim Wilson, a “karaoke clown”.

He withdrew the jibe at the Speaker’s request. But it was an example of an insult used to distract from the greatest problem facing Australians: rising prices are making them poorer.
news.summary: AARON PATRICK: The two leaders are shifting blame for economic problems to the independent agencies responsible for setting interest rates.
news.author: Aaron Patrick

news.title: ‘South Park’ Season 29 Premiere Embraces ‘South America’ Name Change With New Theme Song And a Trump Cameo
news.text:
“South Park” — or rather “South America” — made its Season 29 debut Wednesday night and wasted no time introducing audiences to the newly named town.

 The episode, titled “South American Biker Gangs,” kicked off with an updated theme song ringing in the name change — “I’m goin’ down to South America, have myself a time!” — before showing another new addition: a Donald Trump cameo.

 The premiere episode centered around the usual suspects, Cartman, Stan, Kyle and Kenny, and their newfound love of e-bikes. But when the gaggle of kids takes to the streets with their motorized bikes, the parents of South America form their own biker gang in opposition.

 As per usual, Kenny dies when his e-bike blows up, and his death unites the town to come together, outlaw e-bikes, and begin selling “South America Strong” T-shirts.

 Earlier this month, ahead of the Season 29 premiere, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone announced that the long-running comedy series would furthermore be known as “South America,” a comedic jab at Trump’s recent moves to rename the likes of Lake Ontario as Lake America, New Mexico as New America and the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

 “Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of ‘South Park’ to ‘South America,’” the pair shared in a statement. “We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount — a Skydance Capitulation.”

 The show took home the gold for outstanding animated program at the 2026 Creative Arts Emmys, and while celebrating the win, threw another dig at Trump by sharing a graphic of the president with his pants and underwear around his ankles to the official “South Park” X account.

 The moves are a continuation of the show’s Season 28 political antics, which included plot points like JD Vance seducing Donald Trump in order to dodge punishment for trying to kill his unborn baby with Satan and Pete Hegseth trying to bust Peter Thiel out of jail.

news.title: Miranda Devine: Trump was nearly assassinated more than 2 years ago. We deserve the truth
news.text:
It’s been more than two years since Donald Trump was shot at his campaign rally in Butler, Pa., and the president still has not been given a satisfactory answer for why 20-year-old Thomas Crooks came within a fraction of an inch of assassinating the then-candidate.

It sounds like Trump is angry about it — and he has every right to be.

“Everybody knows the Crooked Joe Biden FBI didn’t do what they should have with respect to the Lunatic who shot me in Butler, PA,” he posted Tuesday morning.

“By the time I got into Office, on January 20th, most of the information was missing, altered, corrupted, or gone.

“New info was just found! Why wasn’t it seen long ago?

“This was all a Democrat Plot, to get me out of the Election, that failed. Dirty Cop Christopher Wray [the director of the FBI at the time] should pay a price for the way he handled this assassination attempt, and certainly for the things he said.”

The White House confirmed the president’s “spray” was prompted by new information about Crooks (pictured at right on the day of the assassination attempt) extracted from the FBI by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and published exclusively in The Post that day.

Who paid for cremation?

Among the revelations is the startling news that an “anonymous donor” paid for the cremation of Crooks’ body after he was killed by a Secret Service sniper moments after he opened fire at the Trump rally on July 13, 2024, striking the then-candidate’s right ear, killing volunteer fire chief Corey Comperatore, and injuring two other rally-goers.

Yet it could be significant, because the cremation destroyed crucial evidence. Rep. Clay Higgins (R-La.), who was part of House Task Force on the Attempted Assassination of Donald J. Trump, described the cremation as “obstruction to any following investigative effort” and said he was informed only a week later when he went to inspect the body.

We don’t know if the FBI questioned the donor to establish a motive for such largesse. It could be simple compassion for the Crooks family — but there could be a sinister reason.

Why hasn’t the FBI ever disclosed this fact, if not to the public then at least to Trump and the Comperatore family?

When I asked the FBI if the -donor had been identified and investigated, an agency flack replied:

“The documents in question are not new — they have been fully investigated by this FBI, briefed to the White House, and were turned over to the [Senate] Judiciary Committee by this FBI 6 months ago.”

If the information is “not new” and was already “briefed to the White House,” why did the president describe it as “new info [that] was just found! Why wasn’t it seen long ago?”

And why have we just learned — from the president — that “most of the information [about Butler] was missing, altered, corrupted, or gone” by the time he took office. Who interfered with it, and why?

As usual, the FBI is not being straight with us.

No wonder the president is dissatisfied. What else has been withheld about the Crooks investigation, and why?

The president also made the alarming claim that the assassination attempt was “all a Democrat Plot, to get me out of the Election, that failed.”

If the president is wrong, he deserves a full accounting of that day that allays his fears.

So does the Comperatore family and the two seriously wounded rally-goers, James Copenhaver and David Dutch, who are suing the federal government for alleged negligence.

And so does the American -public.

The latest trove of files was released by Grassley, in his role as chairman of the Judiciary Committee, as part of his ongoing inquiry into the Butler -assassination attempt.

Slap at the Biden FBI

But why did it take a 93-year-old senator, as legendary as he is, to extract useful information about Crooks? Is he the only person in Washington, DC, with investigative powers?

Judicial Watch’s Tom Fitton isn’t happy about the FBI’s secrecy and sluggish document releases, -either.

He first requested the Crooks files in July 2024 under Freedom of Information laws and was ignored. A year later Fitton was forced to sue the FBI to start producing documents in dribs and drabs. He says at the slow rate they’re going, it will take “12.5 years to produce it all.”

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), a member of Grassley’s committee, is also critical of the lack of transparency.

“I’ve been saying forever now, we have got to have a full accounting of everything that happened on that day,” Hawley told Fox News Digital. “And I still don’t think we’ve gotten a full accounting. Pretty much everything we know about this is from whistleblowers. . . . Otherwise we run the risk of things like this happening again.”

The latest Grassley trove included FBI interviews in July, August and December 2024 with the attempted assassin’s father, Matthew Crooks, who revealed his late son’s obsession with guns and -cybersecurity had accelerated in the period leading up to the -attack.

Matthew unlocked his gun safe and handed his son the gun used to shoot Trump — a few hours before the would-be assassin climbed onto a rooftop and opened fire.

But the documents show that two months beforehand, Matthew had searched online for ways to prevent his son from accessing guns.

The Butler rally was the first public event at which Trump was provided counter-sniper protection, after Secret Service leaders were provided a classified intelligence briefing about an Iranian plot to assassinate the then-presidential candidate.

While there were fatal flaws in the way the Secret Service handled security that day, without the counter-snipers, Thomas Crooks might have achieved his goal, -although a local police officer fired the shot that hit Crooks’ rifle and stopped him from continuing to shoot.

Dems might get gavel

Grassley is approaching the end of his term as chairman of the Judiciary Committee, with hyper-partisan Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) to get the gavel if Democrats take over after the midterms.

That doesn’t bode well for transparency, judging by the twisted priorities in the farcical grilling of FBI Director Kash Patel at a Senate Oversight Committee hearing Tuesday.

Patel testified that Thomas Crooks acted alone.

“We found no evidence that that individual was literally even speaking to any other human being other than his parents, who he resided with,” Patel testified.

But Patel wasn’t asked why the FBI contacted at least one foreign government during its investigation. The senators were more interested in asking stupid questions about bestiality.

We deserve better.
news.summary: We deserve better.
news.author: Miranda Devine

news.title: Trump Admin Denies Palestinian Officials' Visas for 'Glorifying Terrorism'
news.text: The Trump administration has again denied visas to Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas and other senior Palestinian officials ahead of the United Nations General Assembly, blocking the high-level Palestinian delegation from attending in person for the second consecutive year, according to the Associated Press. The State Department said Wednesday that the Palestinian Authority and Palestine Liberation Organization had failed to live up to commitments made to the United States, citing actions it said undermined the prospects for peace, including legal action against Israel at international courts and efforts to seek unilateral recognition. In a statement, the department also cited what it described as continued payments to the families of prisoners convicted of attacks against Israelis and the “glorification” of terrorism and terrorists in public statements and school textbooks. “As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the State Department said. The department said the measures were being imposed under the Middle East Peace Commitments Act of 2002, adding: “It is in our national interest to impose consequences and hold the PLO and PA accountable for glorifying terrorism.” The State Department's announcement did not identify Abbas by name or provide individual visa decisions. Newsweek reached out to the Palestinian Authority by email for comment. What the Sanctions Mean for UNGA The announcement comes less than a week before world leaders gather in New York for the U.N. General Assembly's high-level general debate, which begins September 22. The State Department said it would maintain a “standing waiver” for personnel notified to the PLO Observer Mission to the United Nations, as it has in previous determinations. Despite the visa denials, Palestinians will still be represented at the gathering by diplomats already accredited to the United Nations. Abbas appeared by video at last year's General Assembly after being denied a U.S. visa, following a General Assembly decision allowing Palestine to participate remotely. The General Assembly is expected to vote on a similar measure allowing Abbas to participate remotely again this year, according to The Jerusalem Post. The State Department has taken similar action against foreign officials around UNGA. Last year, Colombian President Gustavo Petro spoke to a crowd outside U.N. headquarters in New York, where he called for an armed force to “free Palestine” and urged U.S. soldiers to disobey President Donald Trump's orders. The State Department subsequently revoked Petro's visa over the remarks. The UN General Assembly is scheduled to take place September 22 to 28 at the United Nations Headquarters in New York. news.summary: The State Department's announcement comes less than a week before the UN General Assembly.
news.author: Alex Backus

news.title: China ready to safeguard Iran’s ‘rights, interests’
news.text:
BEIJING: China is willing to “safeguard Iran’s rights and interests” and to “strengthen dialogue and cooperation”, Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his counterpart Abbas Araghchi during their meeting in Beijing on Wednesday.

Wang Yi said China encourages Iran and the United States to remain rational, exercise restraint, return to the interim peace deal they signed in June and “engage in substantive consultations”.

“We urge all parties to take effective measures to reopen the Strait of Hormuz at an early date” to safeguard the stability of international energy transport and supply chains, the Chinese foreign minister said, adding that China “does not want to see regional tensions to spill over further into Yemen and the Red Sea”.

“We encourage Iran and the US to stay rational and restrained,” he added.

Wang tells Araghchi Beijing doesn’t want regional tensions to spill over into Yemen and Red Sea

Tehran and Washington should “rebuild the negotiation mechanism based on the consensus reached so far”, Wang told Araghchi, who was on a one-day visit to Beijing.

Abbas Araghchi said in his speech Tehran welcomed diplomatic solutions which protect its rights.

“Iran, while fully prepared to powerfully defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and safeguard its security… against aggressors, welcomes diplomatic solutions that ensure the rights of the Iranian nation,” Araghchi said.

The talks between the two diplomats came a week ahead of an expected meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Washington.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier said Trump and Xi would continue discussions on Iran and China’s financial links to Tehran, which Washington has been seeking to shut out of Western financial systems.

Beijing, the main buyer of Iran’s oil, had repeatedly stressed the need to restore normal and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but has largely refrained from directly challenging Tehran’s threats to shipping.

“The current situation once again demonstrates that the existing security architecture in the Middle East is inadequate and needs to be reformed and strengthened,” Wang said in the talks with Araghchi.

China stands ready to promote peace, fairness and justice in the region, and its policy toward Iran has remained consistent and stable, he added.

Damage to US bases

A destroyed aircraft, shredded tents, trailers that have been ripped apart: images taken by US troops show significant damage from Iranian strikes targeting American military assets in the Middle East, CBS News reported on Tuesday.

The undated images were taken at a base in Saudi Arabia and two facilities in Kuwait, according to CBS.

“This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public,” CBS quoted one US service member as saying.

“We’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face,” the service member added.

The Pentagon’s inspector general released a report earlier this week that said the military’s Central Command (Centcom), which is responsible for US forces in the Middle East, had reported widespread damage to American facilities and equipment.

Centcom said Iranian strikes “damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan”, the report said.

The Defence Department estimated the cost of the war at $33.4 billion as of June 29, but that figure “does not include costs for infrastructure repairs”, according to the report.

news.text:

news.title: Iran’s emergence
news.text:
AN especially dangerous moment is opening up as the war in the Middle East transitions gears. The war launched by Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu back in February has effectively ended. It devolved into a stand-off around Hormuz. What is opening up now is something new. And where this takes us is the big unknown.

A big power is emerging to our west. Shackled by sanctions for decades, and threatened incessantly with war, Iran had been walled away from the rest of the world since 1979. But now that America has demonstrated its impotence by failing every military objective it had laid in the war since February, the country that was tied down behind a wall of sanctions is emerging as a big power in the region.

In that sense, what is happening with Iran today is similar to what happened with China following détente. That country, too, was tied down and shackled and shunned by the global community ever since its revolution in 1949. Détente was its negotiated re-entry into the community of nations, and since then, the reforms undertaken within China propelled it to becoming a global power.

Iran’s story differs from this in the sense that it is not going to be a global power. However, it is certainly going to emerge as a regional power in a very important region of the world. Second, Iran’s re-entry into the world community is going to be far more disorderly than that of China, mainly because it has had to fight its way out of the oblivion into which it was banished since the revolution of 1979.

Short of an attempt to destroy its infrastructure, Iran’s emergence as a big power in the region is unstoppable.

But emergence is now underway. It will be a very disorderly, and possibly violent, affair. A lot depends on which faction within Iran manages to rise to the top and take over decision-making. In China, an internal reckoning took place within the Communist Party first, before the reform-minded elements around Deng Xiaoping could rise to the top and take control of the post-opening up trajectory. That is a fraught history, from the Cultural Revolution and the purge of Deng in 1966, to the attempted coup by Lin Biao and his death in a plane crash in Mongolia in 1971, to the rise of Zhou Enlai and the so-called Gang of Four that was ranged against him and the eventual emergence of Deng as the successor, his second purge after Zhou Enlai’s death, and eventual restoration following Mao’s death in 1976.

That is when China firmly embarked on its reformist course and broke its moorings to Mao’s thought. What followed was a carefully calibrated set of measures designed to open the Chinese economy up to the outside world — slowly and experimentally. That trajectory eventually propelled China towards becoming a global power, even if the process took many decades to complete.

Iran is now at a similar point in its trajectory. Following the death of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, and its victory in the war against the Zionist alliance of America and Israel, it now has to go through the internal process of wrangling between rival factions, who must decide whether to remain wedded to the past or break out into a new future. This process will take years to unfold; what makes the Iranian trajectory different from the Chinese one is that in Iran the process will unfold in the context of a war.

It is evident that within Iran there is a pragmatic faction that wants to see the war come to a close and the task of rebuilding the country to begin. But equally important, there is a faction that wants to press ahead with the fighting to deliver a humiliating defeat to the aggressors. This faction wants to do to the Americans in the Middle East what the Taliban, too, did to them in Afghanistan: force a hurried and disorderly flight from the region.

The real game begins after that. Once the Americans leave the region, the Iranian military machine will turn its attention towards the Gulf monarchs. There will be reparations to pay. The bill for the war has already been served. In July 2025, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the Financial Times that there could be no return to nuclear talks until Iran had been compensated for the damage caused by the June war. America scoffed at the demand. In March 2026, the demand was made again in the counter-offer that Iran made to the American proposal for talks. In April, they added an amount — $270 billion — while another figure of $300bn was written into the US-Iran MOU in June 2026.

Nobody should be scoffing at the demand now. In addition to retaining control of Hormuz, Iran will press this demand in the days to come and it is the Gulf monarchs who will be left to pay the bill once the US decides the conflict no longer serves any of its interests. And once the Gulf monarchs settle this amount, another will surface. And then another.

Iran’s emergence as a big power in the region is now unstoppable, short of an attempted catastrophic destruction of the entire country’s infrastructure by the Zionist alliance. This may be an unlikely outcome at this point in time, but it cannot be ruled out. The emergence as a big power is already underway. After consolidating their control on Hormuz, they will next turn their gaze to the riches of the Gulf monarchs. Those riches are now imperilled.

China’s story is instructive here because it tells us that a post-revolutionary polity can manage its affairs to secure its re-entry into the global system of trade, finance and diplomacy to procure maximum benefits for itself. Whether Iran manages this moment similarly, or whether they decide to press their military advantage to the hilt and use their newfound centrality to avenge the past rather than build a future, is the big question hanging over all of us today.

news.title: US House Passes Sweeping Russia Sanctions Bill, Sends It to Trump
news.text:
The US House of Representatives passed a sweeping bipartisan sanctions and tariff package on Wednesday, giving President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy.

The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed by 262 votes to 159 and now heads to Trump’s desk. The Senate approved the measure 86-11 in August.

The legislation is aimed at cutting the financial and logistical networks that help Moscow sustain its war against Ukraine, targeting Russia’s energy sector, defense suppliers, major financial institutions and sanctions-evasion networks.

It also authorizes sanctions against individuals involved in the abduction of Ukrainian children.

Pressure on Russian energy revenues

At the center of the bill is a secondary-tariff mechanism aimed at countries continuing to buy Russian oil and gas.

President Trump would be able to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries purchasing large volumes of Russian energy or helping Moscow evade sanctions. Major buyers such as China and India could be affected, depending on how the measures are implemented.

Supporters say the goal is to reduce the flow of energy revenue that continues to finance Russia’s war.

Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, who worked on the legislation with Graham, described the measures as “scorching sanctions” intended to “throttle Putin’s war machine.”

Banks, shadow fleet and military suppliers

The package also targets Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers used to move crude despite Western restrictions.

It would sanction foreign suppliers supporting Russia’s defense sector, networks helping Moscow circumvent existing measures, and Russian officials and military figures.

New US investment in Russia would also face restrictions, along with exports that could support the Russian military.

Graham’s final sanctions push

The bill is named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Washington’s most prominent supporters of Ukraine and a key architect of the sanctions push.

Graham spent more than a year building support for the legislation before his death in July.

The bill’s passage marks one of Congress’s most consequential recent moves to increase economic pressure on Moscow as Ukraine continues to resist Russia’s full-scale invasion.
news.summary: The House passed a major Russia sanctions package aimed at cutting the financial networks sustaining Moscow’s war against Ukraine and increasing pressure on Putin.

news.title: Trump to host Xi amid pomp, low expectations
news.text:
WASHINGTON, United States: The US military honor guard has been rehearsing and the new White House helipad is ready. But will Xi Jinping and Donald Trump achieve lift-off at their summit next week?

Warnings of an AI apocalypse hang heavy over the Chinese president’s first talks at the White House with his US counterpart, with both countries racing for supremacy in this technology.

Trump’s Iran war casts a long shadow too, as China seeks to avoid US sanctions against countries dealing with Tehran, despite reports that Beijing supplied Tehran with intelligence for a strike on US troops.

A trade war is of even greater concern and the world’s two largest economies are still seeking to mitigate the fallout from Trump’s global tariffs. The threat of war over Taiwan looms large as well.

Behind it all is desire to manage tensions between a superpower keen to keep its place at the top and a rapidly rising rival determined to make the 21st century a Chinese one.

“I’ll be discussing almost everything with him,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday, ahead of their meeting on September 24.

‘Don’t expect much’

But the two leaders are more likely to simply extend a relative truce rather than produce any concrete results, like when Xi hosted Trump in Beijing four months ago, experts said.

“I don’t expect much to come out of this,” Jonathan Czin of the Brookings Institution told AFP.

“In many ways, this is going to be a recapitulation of Trump’s visit to Beijing back in May, where the focus was really on the ostensible rapport between the two leaders.”

With fears about AI making global headlines, agreement to cooperate on regulation or a slowdown is expected to be a major topic of discussion between Trump and Xi.

But any major deals are “politically out of reach for now,” said Wang Dong, a professor at Peking University, as Beijing and Washington both fear losing out in the race for AI dominance.

Tensions over Iran will also come up. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is due to meet his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng this weekend for pre-summit talks including on Iran sanctions.

Trump has, however, played down reports that Chinese entities supplied Iran with satellite imagery for an attack on a US military base in Jordan, saying Xi had “behaved reasonably well” and that “we spy on them, too.”

On trade, there is “room for progress on tariffs, agricultural purchases and selected export controls,” Yue Su of The Economist Intelligence Unit told AFP.

‘Spectacle’

Yet Trump has, as so often before, appeared more interested in the optics of his meeting with a powerful foreign leader than with the substance.

“This is less a summit and more a spectacle. This is designed for deep public consumption,” said Kurt Campbell, former US Deputy Secretary of State and now Chairman of The Asia Group.

Trump pushed for a new granite helicopter landing pad on the White House South Lawn to be open in time for Xi’s visit, which will include a grand state dinner.

Troops in flashy uniforms have been rehearsing on the White House driveway this week ahead of the welcome ceremony.

Trump’s only disappointment is that his under-construction $400 million ballroom won’t be ready — though he has said that when finished it will “top” Beijing’s Great Hall of the People, where Xi hosted him in May.

During the Beijing trip Trump showered praise on Xi, only for the Chinese leader to warn about possible “conflict” over Taiwan.

Fears of a possible Chinese invasion of the self-governing island and global semiconductor hub — which Beijing claims as its territory — remain the most sensitive topic between Washington and Beijing, said Peking University’s Wang.

One possible concrete deliverable is an announcement of further summits.

Trump and Xi are expected to meet in November at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzen, China. The Kremlin has suggested a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump is meanwhile expected to invite Xi to the G20 summit in December at his Doral resort in Miami.

news.title: House Unanimously Votes to Stop Penny Production
news.text:
The House of Representatives has unanimously voted to pass the Common Cents Act, which would send the United States penny into extinction.

Democrats and Republicans voted together on Monday to block the U.S. Treasury from minting any more one-cent coins, and to require any person or business selling goods or services for cash to round “to the nearest amount divisible by five for the payment or transfer of cash.”

If passed by the Senate as expected, the bill will take effect one year after. Pennies already in circulation will remain legal tender, lawmakers clarified. 

The bill was led in the House by Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-MI) and Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), the ranking member of the House Oversight Committee.

The unanimous vote came after the U.S. Mint stopped making new pennies in November 2025, but the legislation would prevent it from restarting the production of pennies in the future. 

Costs associated with producing each penny have risen to 3.69 cents, far outweighing the value they carry. The Treasury stated in a press release that they could annually save $56 million. 

The anti-penny vote came after President Donald Trump instructed Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to have his agency stop making new pennies at the beginning of last year, calling it “wasteful.”

By May 2025, the Treasury had placed its final order for penny blanks, the Wall Street Journal reported.

news.title: US Fed delivers first rate hike since 2023
news.text:
WASHINGTON: The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised interest rates in the world’s largest economy by 25 basis points to tackle stubbornly high inflation, a move sure to anger President Donald Trump, who has demanded lower rates.

The Fed’s Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to raise rates to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent, citing “elevated” inflation and adding that the rate hike would support a “timelier return” to its 2pc target for the metric.

Addressing a press conference after the rate decision, US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh stre-ssed that the central bank’s decision to raise interest rates, the first since 2023, was not influenced by financial markets.

“We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation,” Warsh told the press conference. “I’ll observe market prices and see what they have to say. But today was our decision.” 

He said that the central bank’s independence comes from staying focused on its objectives, in comments that come amid political pressure for lower interest rates. 

“Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane,” Warsh said. “We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too. That’s how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them. 

“Our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long,” he told a press conference.

A majority of Fed policymakers expect at least one more rate hike to be necessary before the end of the year, according to the central bank’s Summary of Economic Projections, also published Wednesday.

news.title: Trump says Kennedy Center could be 'ripped down' without his overhaul
news.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts will "end up being ripped down" without renovations that he's threatened not to carry out unless his name is added to the side of the building.

Trump, speaking to reporters on Sept. 16, defended his position that he be recognized with an honorary inscription below the main sign of the Kennedy Center ‒ a move the center's board approved but a federal judge this week blocked.

"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition," Trump said. "Because, frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad, bad shape, very dangerous shape."

Trump's second term: President Trump threw 'tantrum' during Kennedy Center meeting, congresswoman says

The Kennedy Center's board, composed of mostly Trump loyalists with the president serving as chairman, voted on Sept. 15 to close the iconic institution immediately to undergo two-year renovations that Trump has vowed to help pay for.

Trump and Kennedy Center officials have argued the center's disrepair after years of neglect has turned into a safety threat to guests attending shows. Congress has approved $257 million for renovations. But the Justice Department says without Trump’s additional fundraising aiming for more than $100 million, the work can’t be completed.

"It's been badly maintained for 25 years," Trump said. "I'd like to be able to save but it's going to take a lot of subsidy into the future, and for us as an administration to want to do that, I think the Trump administration should be recognized."

After the board's vote to close the center, Trump warned he won't pursue the renovations unless U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper's decision keeping his name off the center's building is overturned on appeal.

Trump and the Kennedy Center. Judge blocks Kennedy Center's plan to add Trump's name back on building

Cooper ruled the Kennedy Center's plan to add an inscription on the building that says "renovated and restored by Donald J. Trump" cannot move forward. The judge said the inscription violates his previous order in May to remove Trump's name from the center's title and signage and violates the 1964 law that created the center to honor President Kennedy after his assassination.

The Justice Department has appealed the decision on Trump's honorary inscription.

Cooper is expected to later rule whether the temporarily closure of the Kennedy Center also violates his previous order. The judge, in the same May order, blocked the Kennedy Center board's vote in March to close for two years, citing a lack of adequate information before the rushed action.

news.title: Detroit News Endorses Mike Rogers as ‘Clearly the Best Choice’ for U.S. Senate in Michigan
news.text:
The Detroit News endorsed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race on Wednesday, pointing to his experience in Congress, the military, and the FBI.

“Mike Rogers is clearly the best choice for Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat and gets our endorsement.”

The newspaper’s editorial board described Rogers as well prepared for the Senate after serving 14 years in the House, including a stint as chairman of the House Intelligence Committee.

Rogers, 63, left Congress in 2015 after representing a mid-Michigan district for seven terms. He later worked in the private sector, focusing on cybersecurity. He previously served as an Army officer and an FBI agent investigating organized crime.

The editorial argued that Rogers’s background and temperament could help him quickly become an influential member of the Senate.

The newspaper was critical of his Democrat opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, saying he lacks the government and policymaking experience needed for the job.

El-Sayed, 41, previously led the Detroit Health Department and later served as director of Wayne County’s Department of Health, Human, and Veterans Services. He holds medical and public health degrees and previously taught epidemiology at Columbia University, though he is not licensed to practice medicine.

The editorial board also accused El-Sayed of trying to conceal parts of his past by removing social media posts and about 100 YouTube videos ahead of the Senate race. It said those actions made it difficult for voters to determine what he truly believes.

The newspaper further raised concerns about El-Sayed’s ties to the Democratic Party’s far-left wing, citing his support from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and his association with socialist political figures. It also criticized his position on Israel and his decision to campaign with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.

The editorial acknowledged that Rogers’ endorsement from President Donald Trump could hurt him with Michigan voters. A recent Detroit News/WDIV-TV poll found Trump deeply unpopular in the state.

However, the board argued that voters should consider the full six-year Senate term instead of using the race to register their opposition to Trump, who is set to leave office two years into the term.

news.title: Feds Charge Mexican National Arrested at Texas Border With Helping Terrorist Drug Cartel
news.text:
A 21-year-old Mexican national arrested at the Texas border faces terrorism charges for allegedly working as a hitman for a Mexican cartel, U.S. Department of Justice officials announced Sept. 16.

Jose Flores-Flores, of Tamaulipas, Mexico, was charged with federal counts related to providing material support to the foreign terrorist organization the Cartel del Golfo, also known as the Gulf cartel.

He was also charged with illegal reentry into the United States, being in the United States after previously being deported, and giving false information to border agents, according to court documents.

He was arrested at the border on July 10 with two other illegal border crossers, according to authorities. Before the arrest, he was questioned by a Border Patrol agent who noticed inconsistencies with Flores-Flores’s age and discovered he was an adult and had been convicted in January 2025 for illegally entering the United States, according to authorities.

President Donald Trump assigned the terrorist designation to the Gulf Cartel last year, giving law enforcement more tools to prosecute criminals accused of crimes related to cartel activity.

“That designation matters,” Rio Grande Section Chief Patrol Agent Jared Ashby said at a press conference held in McAllen, Texas. “It recognizes the serious national security threat posed by these organizations and gives prosecutors additional tools to pursue charges when supported by the evidence.”

U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz said Flores-Flores has been an alleged active member of the cartel for more than a year.

Investigators reviewed Flores-Flores’s phone for evidence and discovered photos of “piles of chopped up body parts” and images of the defendant allegedly holding military-style radios and weapons.

They also allegedly found a video of the defendant dismembering a corpse, Reitz said.

Flores-Flores told investigators he was a “sakario,” which means a hitman or contract killer.

“What’s more, he admitted that it was, in fact, him seen in the gruesome images and videos on his phone,” Reitz said. “He described his job as a ranger and hitman for the Gulf Cartel, driving around looking for targets, monitoring Mexican authorities, and rival cartels’ communications,” Reitz said. “And when a body needed to be chopped up, Flores-Flores was the guy you called.”

According to prosecutors, the defendant allegedly worked nights for the Los Metros faction of the cartel, maintaining his assigned sector in Reynosa, Mexico, a border city across the Rio Grande from McAllen, Texas. He allegedly conducted counter-surveillance against the Mexican military and law enforcement.

Investigators allege Flores-Flores dismembered at least two people on the outskirts of Reynosa after they ran afoul of the cartel.

Evidence found by Border Patrol helped identify suspected human disposal locations in Mexico, revealing three sets of human remains in possible grave sites, according to Ashby.

Flores-Flores is the first illegal immigrant apprehended by the agency to face federal terrorism charges for his alleged role in supporting a designated foreign terrorist organization, the Rio Grande sector chief said.

Flores-Flores is scheduled to be arraigned before a magistrate judge on Sept. 24, according to prosecutors.

He faces up to 20 years in federal prison and a possible $250,000 maximum fine.

Flores-Flores’s federal public defender in McAllen, Texas, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about the charges.

Another member of the same cartel was arrested earlier this year in Texas.

The trooper tried to stop a vehicle for a traffic violation in Rio Grande City when the driver refused to stop, resulting in a high-speed chase through rural neighborhoods.

Juan Gonzalez, 24, of Rio Grande City, Texas, was charged with three counts of human smuggling and evading arrest. The three illegal immigrants who fled from the vehicle during the chase were handed over to Border Patrol.

Investigators confirmed Gonzalez as a member of the Gulf cartel with ties to the group operating in Miguel Aleman, Mexico. He was taken into federal custody.
news.summary: Jose Flores-Flores allegedly worked as a hitman for the Gulf cartel in a Mexican border city.
news.author: Jill McLaughlin

news.title: Trump: Iran ‘Very Much’ Wants a Deal, Reached Out ‘Directly’ — ‘Hopefully’ Nearing End of War
news.text:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that Iran has contacted the United States “directly” and “very much” wants a deal, expressing hope that the nearly seven-month conflict is approaching its end after predicting last week that the fighting would conclude following November’s midterm elections.

“Hopefully we’re toward the end of the war,” Trump told reporters after arriving in North Carolina, responding to a question about what phase the conflict had reached.

Trump then turned to the prospect of an agreement with Tehran.

“Iran is very much wanting to make a deal,” he said. “We’ll see how that works out.”

Asked moments later whether he had recently heard from Iran directly or through intermediaries, Trump replied: “Directly.”

The disclosure follows a series of increasingly explicit statements from Trump that the conflict could be approaching its end. Last week, he predicted the fighting would conclude following the November midterm elections, arguing that Tehran could no longer sustain the pressure.

“I think the war will end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer,” Trump said.

By Monday, Trump was publicly describing Tehran as actively seeking an agreement while leaving the decision over renewed engagement to Washington.

“The failing Nation of Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “I will determine whether or not the U.S.A. will choose to engage — the concept of which we are open to.”

Vice President JD Vance reinforced that emerging end-state Tuesday, declaring the “first phase” of the U.S. campaign complete and saying the conflict would enter a “much different phase” within months as Washington shifts toward preventing Tehran from rebuilding the capabilities destroyed since fighting began Feb. 28.

“There are really two phases to this thing, and the first phase is done,” Vance said.

Vance described the opening phase as the destruction of Iran’s nuclear program and the severe degradation of its conventional military and ability to project power.

The next task, he explained, is to “ensure that they’re not able to rebuild and try to maintain as much global stability in the wake of that.”

Vance also backed Trump’s assessment that the conflict could change substantially following the midterms, while emphasizing that the president will ultimately determine when the campaign ends.

“We can’t predict the future, but I think the president is right to say that this thing will enter a much different phase in a couple of months,” Vance said. Trump, he added, “is the person who determines … when conflicts start and when they stop.”

The administration is already preparing for what could follow the current phase of the conflict. Trump is expected to meet with Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York next Tuesday to discuss the next steps in the war, Axios reported Wednesday, citing three sources with direct knowledge.

The meeting is expected to include discussions of U.S. ideas for a postwar strategy as Trump and his senior team develop a “day-after” plan expected to be finalized following the midterm elections, according to the outlet. The State Department sent initial invitations Wednesday to leaders or foreign ministers from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman, with the gathering potentially expanding to other Arab and Muslim countries.

The diplomatic signals come as Washington continues applying military and economic pressure aimed both at preventing Tehran from rebuilding its military capabilities and further isolating the regime from the global economy.

CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said Wednesday that internationally recognized shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz remain free of mines, with U.S. forces staying “present and watchful” to keep them clear.

“The strait is open, those lanes are open, and that is why commercial vessels continue to flow through them,” Hawkins said, describing the U.S. blockade against Iran as “ironclad.”

CENTCOM said Tuesday that U.S. forces had redirected 103 commercial vessels under the blockade, while Hawkins said Wednesday that the military has helped facilitate commercial traffic carrying more than 900 million barrels of crude through Hormuz since early May.

Washington is simultaneously tightening its effort to cut Tehran off financially. Treasury on Wednesday convened global financial institutions under Operation Economic Outcast, providing them information aimed at shutting down revenue streams and procurement networks tied to the Iranian regime.

“Treasury continues to sever every economic lifeline Tehran has left,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said, adding that financial institutions were working “in lockstep with the U.S. government” to support the campaign.

Treasury said its collaboration with the private sector is intended to ensure there is “no space for the Iranian regime to rebuild its capacity” to threaten the United States and the wider world.

Even as Trump increasingly points toward an end to the fighting, he has made clear that any agreement with Tehran would extend well beyond the nuclear restrictions Washington sought before the conflict.

“I’m doing much more than a nuclear deal,” Trump said last week. “There’s a lot more than nuclear.”

Trump said additional demands would now be on the table, which Washington had not been pursuing three months earlier, underscoring how dramatically the terms of any renewed diplomacy have shifted after nearly seven months of U.S. military and economic pressure.

Joshua Klein is a reporter for Breitbart News. Email him at jklein@breitbart.com. Follow him on Twitter @JoshuaKlein.

President Donald Trump said Wednesday that Iran has contacted the United States “directly” and “very much” wants a deal, expressing hope that the nearly seven-month conflict is approaching its end after predicting last week that the fighting would conclude following November’s midterm elections.
