news.title: Trump Revokes 2009 Chesapeake Bay Order
news.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Wednesday that puts an end to a 17-year-old Chesapeake Bay mandate. Federal Cabinet departments, under the order, are to shift support to projects that demonstrate the ability to reduce runoff.

Dated Sept. 16, the order cancels Executive Order 13508 from May 12, 2009, which the White House says told states and cities to help restore the bay but without providing details on how to do so. Local governments used that order as a basis for levying stormwater fees, often called rain taxes, that the new order says can run to hundreds of dollars a year for households and small businesses.

Nothing in the 2009 text required those fees, according to Wednesday’s order. States nevertheless used them to pay for stormwater systems, “whether or not it contributes to the environmental health of the Chesapeake Bay.”

Federal, state, and local environmental work since 2009 has already moved the numbers in a positive direction, according to the order. As of 2025, the watershed jurisdictions had met 100 percent of their sediment-reduction goal, 90 percent of the phosphorus goal, and 57 percent of the nitrogen goal. These jurisdictions include New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, the District of Columbia, Delaware, and West Virginia.

The order says that work has restored thousands of acres of reefs and lines up with the 2025 revised Chesapeake Bay Watershed Agreement, which the federal government and the agencies named in the new directive.

Scientists from the College of William & Mary, the Virginia Institute of Marine Science, FlowWest, and the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science reported in 2026 that the bay’s annual dead zone is projected to be among the smallest since 1985, about 31 percent below the long-term average.

Given that record, the White House said it made sense to pull the old order.

Cabinet secretaries at War, Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, and Homeland Security, plus the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator, must review what their departments now spend on the bay. Fiscal and staff resources are to go to “more direct, on-the-ground projects, in areas of highest need.”

Any agency still directing funds toward the bay has to peel money off work that can’t show progress and direct it toward projects that reduce nutrient and sediment runoff into the bay and the rivers that feed it.

The EPA gets a separate assignment under the executive order: sit down with Maryland, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Delaware, New York, West Virginia and the District of Columbia. That means assessing what stormwater fees cost residents, looking for ways to protect the bay without raising household bills, and taking steps to encourage states and localities to repeal those fees.

What follows from the order is designed to rely on verifiable numbers—sediment, phosphorus, and nitrogen content, and water quality improvement.

The White House fact sheet that went out with the order states that the EPA, in fiscal 2026, streamlined the Chesapeake Bay Program, folded assistance agreements together, and shaved nearly $1 million off yearly administrative spending. Those reforms enabled the EPA to award the six watershed states and the District of Columbia $2.7 million more than in fiscal 2025.

The order does not create a private right to sue for violations. It runs subject to existing law and available appropriations. The EPA covers the cost of its publication.

Sen. Ben Cardin (D-Md.) said at the time that while the dead zone was shrinking, urban and suburban runoff into the bay was still climbing and oyster crops were “still not even close to their historic levels.”
news.summary: The directive scraps an Obama-era mandate the White House said states used to justify stormwater 'rain taxes.'
news.author: Kimberly Hayek

news.title: Modi @76. And he never had it easy
news.text: A war in the Middle East, and the one between Russia and Ukraine continuing, punitive tariffs by the US, soaring oil prices, inflation due to supply constraints and an uncertain world order. For Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 2026 has brought together a big set of challenges, with the government led by him doing it all to cushion India from global headwinds. And India has done much better than many other big economies.Everyone thinks 2026 is the year PM Modi is facing huge challenges. Alongside the geopolitical headwinds, the PM Modi-led government faced an youth-led agitation by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which culminated in the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as Union Education Minister in July.Pradhan's exit marked a rare political setback for the government. His resignation came after weeks of protests over NEET-UG 2026 paper leaks and demands for accountability, making it only the second instance since 2014 of a sitting Union minister leaving the Modi government amid public pressure. This year, the BJP-led central government also witnessed a backlash by the "upper castes", which traditionally support the saffron camp, over the UGC Equity Regulations.But if this feels like the toughest phase of Modi's political life, a look at his journey shows that the road, at least from the 1990s, was never smooth.Prime Minister Narendra Modi turns 76 today.A look at his political career shows a pattern of setbacks, rebellions, isolation and bounce backs. Long before he became the country's most recognisable political face, PM Modi was a Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) pracharak, doing the most basic chores at the organisation's office in Ahmedabad.He went underground during the Emergency in 1975, was pushed out of Gujarat politics at the height of his organisational career, spent nearly two years in political isolation, and when he finally became the chief minister of Gujarat, he struggled even to find a constituency from which to enter the Assembly.Then came the Gujarat riots of 2002, the political storm that threatened his chief ministership, years of legal scrutiny and international condemnation, including the US decision in 2005 to deny him a diplomatic visa and revoke his existing touristbusiness visa.Yet each hurdle became another chapter in the Modi political journey as he overcame them. The crusader: For the first time, the Bharatiya Janta Party achieved a full majority and formed the government in the Centre in 2014 under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. (Image: AFP via Getty)THE 1970s: MODI'S JOURNEY FROM SWEEPING FLOORS TO GOING UNDERGROUNDThe story begins far from the Prime Minister's Office in New Delhi.Born in Vadnagar on September 17, 1950, Modi grew up in a family of modest means and helped at the family's tea stall. He joined the RSS as a pracharak in the early 1970s and gradually moved into full-time organisational work. His early years were hardly glamorous. According to senior journalist Arvind Chaturvedi's book, The Real Modi: The Man Who Would be Prime Minister, the prime minister who was then an RSS worker held responsibilities that included preparing tea and breakfast and doing routine work at the organisation's office.Then came the Emergency imposed by the then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.When the Congress government imposed the Emergency in June 1975, the RSS was banned and its activists and workers were forced underground. Modi, then a young RSS worker, became involved in the underground resistance in Gujarat. He travelled in disguise, helped maintain networks of safe houses and distributed anti-Emergency literature. According to various accounts of the period, they describe him appearing in different disguises, once as a Sikh, to avoid arrest during the Emergency.It was an early lesson in political survival for the politician who is currently the longest-serving elected head of government in the country.But bigger tests were still waiting to come for the 25-year-old RSS pracharak. Incognito moment: PM Modi, who was in 1975 working for the RSS, concealed his real identity and amplified the anti-Emergency literature. (Image: File)THE 1990s: FROM BUILDING CADRE TO FACING BANISHMENT FROM GUJARATBy the mid-1990s, Modi had become an important organisational figure in Gujarat BJP politics. That influence, however, also became a source of friction that eventually backfired.In the book Narendra Modi: The Man, The Times, author and journalist Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay described that Modi was accused of interfering in the functioning of the BJP government despite not holding a constitutional office. The perception among some leaders was that he was exercising influence from outside the government — effectively attempting to drive the administration from the back seat."Modi was accused of interfering in government functioning without being a part of it and also for promoting factionalism in the party. At that time, the RSS ensured that though he beat a hasty retreat from Gujarat politics, he was not cast away," Mukhopadhyay wrote in his 2013 book.These tensions exploded in 1995. Keshubhai Patel had become Gujarat's first BJP chief minister after the party's electoral breakthrough. Modi was an aide of Keshubhai.Gujarat BJP leader Shankersinh Vaghela rebelled against Keshubhai and took a large group of MLAs to Khajuraho in Madhya Pradesh while the chief minister was away in the United States.The rebellion produced the now-famous political labels: Hazoorias for Keshubhai loyalists and Khajurias for Vaghela's camp.The central leadership eventually brokered a compromise to save the BJP government in Gujarat. The price was heavy. Keshubhai had to step aside and Modi had to leave Gujarat in form of a political exile as Suresh Mehta took over as the CM.Mukhopadhyay, in his book, quotes Modi himself, describing the compromise as, "Keshubhai would go, and Modi would go out of Gujarat".For the rising organiser, it was more than a transfer. It was "humiliation". The setback: Senior BJP leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee (L) asked Narendra Modi (C) to leave Gujarat and Keshubhai Patel to resign from the post of chief minister after a growing rebellion within the party in 1995. (Image: India Today Group)MODI'S 18 MONTHS OF POLITICAL EXILE, BUILT NETWORKS IN NORTHERN INDIA"Aapda ko avsar me badalna hoga (we will have to convert adversity into opportunity)," said Modi as the PM during the Covid pandemic in 2020. However, he had walked that path long before the talk.As part of his political exile, Modi was sent to Delhi and Chandigarh as a national secretary by the BJP top brass. On paper, it was a party assignment. Politically, however, it was a very different story.Modi's removal from Gujarat was seen by his opponents as evidence that he had overplayed his hand. In the 18-month period, Modi was "lonely and virtually friendless", facing a major political setback and public humiliation despite years of organisational work."When [Atal Bihari] Vajpayee got the party to endorse the compromise package in 1995 that led to Modi being ejected from Gujarat, it was a tacit acceptance of the party that he had overplayed his hand," Mukhopadhyay wrote."In Modi's version, this was a humiliation of sorts because his adversaries wasted no time in contending during conversations with journalists that his posting outside the state was not a promotion but an action of being sidelined. For the next eighteen months, Narendra Modi was lonely and virtually friendless," he added in his book Narendra Modi: The Man, The Times.It was a strange interlude in the career of an RSS pracharak who was sent to the BJP in 1987, and who would eventually dominate Indian politics.There was no Gujarat government to influence. No chief minister's office. No personal electoral constituency. No mass political base. There was only the organisation, a setback and time.The gates of Gujarat were closed for Modi, but he had not disappeared. He built the party network and strengthened the party in the northern parts of India. The grind: In this image, Narendra Modi (L) and BJP veteran Murli Manohar Joshi hoisting the tricolour at Srinagar's Lal Chowk, Jammu and Kashmir in 1992. (Image: India Today Group)MODI'S HOMECOMING: WHEN A CHIEF MINISTER STRUGGLED TO FIND A SEATSix years later in 2001, the same Gujarat that had pushed Modi out would become the stage for his biggest political gamble.By 2001, the BJP government under Keshubhai Patel was struggling amid political discontent, electoral setbacks and criticism of its handling of the aftermath of the devastating Bhuj earthquake. The situation was so bad in Gujarat for the BJP that it started reflecting in the local body polls. The central leadership led by former PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee eventually decided to replace Keshubhai.On October 7, 2001, the 51-year-old Modi was sworn in as Gujarat's chief minister. But there was an immediate problem. Modi had never contested an election.A chief minister who was not an MLA had six months to enter the state legislature. Finding him a safe seat was therefore important and urgent.Modi wanted Ellis Bridge, a BJP bastion in Ahmedabad represented by Haren Pandya, who was given a cabinet berth in 1998 under the Keshubhai-led government after Modi insisted on proposing his name.Pandya, who had his own political standing and constituency base, did not vacate the seat. Even a request from LK Advani did not change his mind."Modi expected his one-time protege [Haren Pandya] to remain loyal when he was evicted from Gujarat. But Pandya shifted his loyalty to Sanjay Joshi and through him to Keshubhai," Mukhopadhyay noted in his book.The eventual solution to the seat dilemma came from Rajkot.Vajubhai Vala, who was the finance minister of Gujarat, vacated the Rajkot-II seat, allowing Modi to contest his first election. The 51-year-old CM won the February 2002 by-election and entered the Gujarat Assembly.But the victory itself was hardly the triumphant coronation that hindsight might suggest. His winning margin was smaller than the BJP's previous margin there, while the party lost two other by-elections held along with the Rajkot seat, which Modi contested.The new chief minister had cleared his first electoral hurdle. He had barely settled into office when Gujarat was engulfed in catastrophe. Blockbuster comeback: Narendra Modi (C) was replaced with Keshubhai Patel (R) as the chief minister of Gujarat after BJP faced massive backlash in the state following the Bhuj earthquake. (Image: India Today Group)2002 GODHRA RIOTS THAT COULD HAVE ENDED EVERYTHINGThe Godhra train burning in February 2002 was followed by devastating communal violence across Gujarat.The violence became the defining controversy of Modi's political career. He faced fierce criticism from opposition parties, sections of the media and civil society over the government's handling of the violence. The political pressure reached the BJP's highest levels.Then-Prime Minister Vajpayee publicly spoke of "raj dharma", the duty of a ruler to govern without discrimination. By April, Modi's political survival was in question.At the BJP National Executive meeting in Goa, he offered to resign as chief minister. The resignation was not accepted.Modi was cleared of charges related to the 2002 Godhra riots by the Supreme Court in 2012, but then in 2002, the episode could have ended his Gujarat career.Instead, the chief minister stayed. The controversy did not disappear. It followed him for years.Even after blowback, Gujarat became the place where Modi began constructing a new political identity for the country — the Gujarat Model — one centred on development, investment and administrative performance alongside his existing ideological appeal. The mass leader: Chief Minister Narendra Modi became a household name in Gujarat and won Assembly elections for three consecutive terms. (Image: India Today Group)REBELLIONS NEVER STOPPED IN GUJARAT, MODI WAS SET FOR DELHISurviving the 2002 crisis did not mean Modi overcame all challenges in Gujarat BJP.Keshubhai Patel remained a source of internal opposition against CM Modi in Gujarat within the BJP. Shankersinh Vaghela had already broken away. Former CM Sanjay Joshi, RSS leader Pravin Togadia and other figures represented different points of friction around Modi's growing authority.There were tensions with sections of the RSS hierarchy too. Modi had risen through the organisation, but once he occupied executive power, the relationship changed.Then came the phase of Modi's political journey that would eventually take him from Gujarat to Delhi. The transformation was gradual.The Gujarat chief minister increasingly presented himself not merely as a Hindutva politician but as a development-oriented administrator. The Vibrant Gujarat summits, investment pitches and emphasis on infrastructure and governance helped build the "Vikas Purush" image around him.By the early 2010s, the political equation inside the BJP started changing. The statesman: As the head of Gujarat's government and later the Centre, Narendra Modi has not only delivered electoral victories but has also built a strong public profile around his policy initiatives. (Image: India Today Group)2012 VICTORY IN GUJARAT, MODI BECAME BJP'S PM FACELK Advani remained the party's most senior national leader, but Modi's political reach had begun extending far beyond Gujarat. His third consecutive Gujarat election victory in 2012 strengthened his claim to a national role.The following year, that possibility became reality and everything changed from then on for the BJP and Indian politics.On September 13, 2013, the BJP formally announced Modi as its prime ministerial candidate for the 2014 Lok Sabha election. The journey from the RSS office floor to the BJP's top national post had taken decades.It had passed through a tea stall, underground safe houses, party rebellions, political exile, an unwanted transfer, a chief minister's seat without an electoral constituency, the Gujarat riots, resignation drama, international condemnation and repeated internal battles.And that is why the story of Modi at 76 is not simply the story of power.It is the story of a septuagenarian who spent much of his career operating under pressure, sometimes from opponents, sometimes from allies, sometimes from his own party and, at crucial moments, from the organisation that had helped build him.The challenges have changed over the decades.The young pracharak once worried about arrest. The BJP organiser worried about being pushed out. The chief minister fought for political survival. The Gujarat leader fought to establish his own model and authority. The prime minister has faced an entirely different scale of pressure.The challenges have just become monstrous since he was re-elected in 2019. The two years of the Covid pandemic and lockdowns were followed by the Russia-Ukraine war. The second stint of Donald Trump as US President saw India being targeted with punitive tariffs. Then there was the Pahalgam terrorist attack and the four-day war with Pakistan in May 2025. Then came the Iran-US war that jeopardised energy supplies from the Middle East.The pattern remains familiar. The challenges, some temporary setbacks and then the bounce backs. news.title: How to Watch the ‘South Park’ Season 29 Premiere on TV and Streaming
news.text:
“South Park” is back with new jokes, new episodes and a new name.

The 29th season of Trey Parker and Matt Stone’s adult comedy — now retitled “South America” in a dig at the Trump administration’s repeated renaming efforts — premieres on TV and streaming on Wednesday. 

This comes hot on the heels of Season 27 winning Outstanding Animated Series at the Creative Arts Emmys (the season started in July 2025, while Season 28 ran from October to December). The show won five Emmys from 2005 to 2013, but had gotten eight nominations with zero wins from 2013 to this year’s ceremony.

This latest win was quite the statement from the Emmys, rewarding the show for the first time in over a decade for a politically charged season that took aim at Donald Trump (portraying him as being literally in bed with Satan), JD Vance and more. The “South Park” team then mocked Trump on social media, congratulating the two-time Emmy loser for finally bringing a statue home.

With all that in mind, Season 29 is sure to be a barnburner. But when do new episodes premiere, and where can you watch them? Read on to find out.

When does “South Park” Season 29 premiere?

“South Park” Season 29 premieres Wednesday, Sept. 16, at 10 p.m. ET/PT with a new episode titled “South American Biker Gangs.”

Where can you watch “South Park” Season 29?

“South Park” Season 29 will premiere on Comedy Central every other Wednesday through Nov. 25. All episodes will stream the day after their premiere on Paramount+.

What is the “South Park” premiere about?

“When e-bikes arrive in South America, the boys take over the streets and the parents of South America can hardly recognize South America,” a plot description reads.

Why is the show called “South America”?

If you didn’t know about “South Park’s” name change, that plot description might’ve been a bit confusing.

In early September, ahead of Season 29, Parker and Stone announced that the new season of “South Park” would see the show take on a new name: “South America.” This change was a clear dig at the Trump administration’s attempted renaming of geographical sites like the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario to the Gulf of America and Lake America.

“Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of ‘South Park’ to ‘South America,’” Parker and Stone said in a statement at the time. “We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount — a Skydance Capitulation.”

news.title: Charlie Kirk's family says officials failed to protect him before attack
news.text:
The family of slain conservative influencer Charlie Kirk has blamed Utah officials for his death at a state university. 

Mr Kirk was shot dead by a rooftop sniper on September 10, 2025, while debating students in an outdoor courtyard.

A wrongful death notice now filed by his family has said "negligence" by Utah Valley University failed to protect the 31-year-old while on their campus.

"The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk's close friend and political ally … the previous year," the notice read.

The shooting happened during his largest campus tour, dubbed "The American Comeback Tour" by Mr Kirk's conservative organisation, Turning Point USA.

The tour, the document added, came with a "backdrop of risk".

"Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the [university] created a foreseeable danger to Charlie," the notice said.

'Fishbowl' scene of Kirk's campus shooting death

Mr Kirk had been debating students in the courtyard, which was surrounded by tall buildings "and other elevated observations".

According to the wrongful death notice, this allegedly "walk[ed] him into a fishbowl".

An Associated Press review following the shooting showed the campus in Orem did not use several public safety practices that have become standard safeguards at events around the country.

Campus police staffing was far below recommended levels for a school of that size.

They also did not fly a drone to monitor rooftops or coordinate with local law enforcement to secure the event attended by about 3,000 people.

There were no bag checks or metal detectors and no first responders immediately available.

This, they alleged, resulted in Mr Kirk being taken to a nearby hospital in a private vehicle, rather than an ambulance.

The wrongful death notice is a required step under state law before his family can file a formal claim or lawsuit.

It names the university and its then-president, Astrid Tuminez, the campus police department and its chief, Jeffrey Long, and the state of Utah.

A spokesperson for Utah Valley University said the school was aware of the notice and would address it "consistent with our established processes".

The Utah Attorney General's Office said it would not comment on potential litigation.

One year after death, trial continues for alleged shooter

The 23-year-old charged with shooting Mr Kirk dead has pleaded not guilty. 

Prosecutors have been granted permission to seek the death penalty for Tyler Robinson, a former apprentice electrician. 

Mr Robinson faces seven charges, including aggravated murder for endangering the lives of others at the event. 

It was unclear when a trial would go forward. The next court hearing has been scheduled for October 23. 

Mr Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, made multiple high-profile appearances, including alongside US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, in the wake of her husband's death. 

Ms Kirk has since been elected chief executive of Turning Point USA. 

One year after the attack, bells tolled at 12.20pm local time at Utah Valley University, marking the time of Mr Kirk's death. 

Outside Turning Point USA's Arizona headquarters, a 2.4-meter-tall statue of Mr Kirk was unveiled to mark the anniversary. 

Three days later, the statue and a nearby poster memorial were found vandalised with red spray-paint.
news.summary: The family of slain podcaster Charlie Kirk has blamed officials at the university campus where he was killed for his death.
news.author: Brianna Morris-Grant

news.title: Mitch McConnell’s Senate Vote Under Scrutiny After Lengthy Health Absence
news.text: Republican Mitch McConnell returned to the Senate this week after a three-month absence, but a brief moment during Wednesday’s Farm Bill vote has raised fresh questions about the 84-year-old senator's fitness to participate in the final months of his congressional career. Video from the Senate Agriculture Committee’s vote shows McConnell sitting in a wheelchair as his name is called during the roll call. He does not immediately respond. Senator Amy Klobuchar, a Democrat from Minnesota, appeared to prompt him. Committee Chairman John Boozman, a Republican from Arkansas, then leaned toward McConnell and appeared to say something to him. McConnell ultimately responded with a quiet “aye.” The clip prompted concern and criticism over whether McConnell was fit to return to the Senate after his lengthy absence and health concerns. McConnell was the tie-breaking vote in the Farm Bill, which passed 12–11 on Wednesday, restoring Republicans’ ability to move the legislation forward after McConnell’s prolonged absence. McConnell later said in a post on X that he was “proud to vote yes” on the legislation and praised provisions affecting Kentucky farmers. He did not respond to questions from reporters on Capitol Hill. Newsweek has reached out to McConnell's office for comment via email. McConnell's Three-Month Absence McConnell's absence began June 14, when he was hospitalized after a fall at his Washington-area home. For weeks, his office offered few details beyond saying he was receiving care and continuing to work with staff. That silence fueled speculation about his condition and prompted increasing calls for transparency. By July, Democratic Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear publicly asked McConnell to provide an update on his health and, if he could not demonstrate he could perform his duties, to consider resigning. Beshear also contacted Senate Majority Leader John Thune about the issue. McConnell eventually disclosed that he had been briefly unconscious after the fall and had also been treated for mild pneumonia. A Capitol physician said McConnell had experienced several falls during the year and attributed some of his mobility problems to his history of childhood polio. The physician said a comprehensive evaluation found no fracture, stroke, hemorrhage, tumor or cardiac abnormality. McConnell was subsequently moved to a rehabilitation facility and was discharged in early August to continue physical therapy at home. During the absence, he continued communicating with staff about Senate and Kentucky matters, according to his office. But he missed votes and remained largely out of public view. The prolonged absence and limited information about McConnell's health have generated increasing pressure in Kentucky. McConnell eventually returned to Washington on Monday. He arrived in a wheelchair and acknowledged that he was still recovering. “My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process,” McConnell said in a released statement, adding that the “lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier. I’m still not quite back to 100percent." But McConnell also made clear that he intended to work. “I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me,” he said. The result was a growing debate not simply about McConnell's health, but about the obligations of an elected official who is unable to appear in Washington for an extended period. His First Vote Back Was Already Consequential McConnell's first Senate vote after the absence came Monday, when he voted for Matthew Byrne, President Donald Trump’s nominee for a federal district judgeship in Ohio. His vote was decisive on the procedural measure. That was followed two days later by the Farm Bill vote. With Republicans holding extremely narrow margins on several committees, one senator's physical presence can change whether legislation moves at all. McConnell's absence had already affected the Agriculture and Appropriations committees, where Republicans and Democrats were otherwise evenly divided. Without him, Republicans were unable to advance some legislation. His absence also came at a consequential moment for the Senate. The chamber is confronting the September 30 government-funding deadline. McConnell remains chairman of the Senate Rules Committee and holds a senior position on the Appropriations Committee, including the defense appropriations subcommittee. His ability to participate matters not only on the floor but inside committees where legislation can be stopped before it ever reaches a final vote. Pressure Builds For McConnell to Stand Down Democrats have increasingly questioned whether the longtime Kentucky senator can continue fulfilling his responsibilities after a three-month health-related absence, while conservative critics have seized on his return to the Capitol — and particularly Wednesday's Farm Bill vote — to question whether he is capable of independently participating in Senate business. McConnell already announced that he would not seek reelection. His Senate term ends in January 2027. After footage of the Farm Bill vote emerged, conservative commentator Nick Sortor shared the clip on X, describing McConnell as a “PUPPET SENATOR” and writing that the senator had to be “TOLD how to vote.” Former Republican Representative Matt Gaetz added in another X post that “Mitch McConnell will be wheeled in and out of the votes needed to stop the Trump agenda.” Melanie D’Arrigo, a former Democratic congressional candidate, wrote that the episode “feels like elder abuse,” invoking the movie Weekend at Bernie’s. Meanwhile, Beshear has been among the most prominent voices questioning whether McConnell is capable of returning to the Senate and has explicitly called on him to prove his “capacity to serve” or resign. The governor previously said McConnell owed Kentuckians an explanation about his condition and whether he could perform his responsibilities. Even late-night television joined the reaction. Jimmy Kimmel joked about McConnell’s appearance, while The Daily Show’s Josh Johnson mocked footage of McConnell being wheeled from the Capitol. What Role Will McConnell Play in His Final Months? McConnell's return coincides with some key votes in the Senate where the GOP holds the majority by a narrow margin. In the coming weeks and months, the Farm Bill will move toward consideration by the full Senate, while lawmakers face a September 30 deadline to fund the government. Defense appropriations will continue moving through Congress, and McConnell has signaled that foreign policy remains a priority, including strengthening NATO and countering Russian aggression against Ukraine. McConnell did not promise to attend every vote when he returned to Washington. Instead, he said he would “do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me.” That could mean McConnell may be seen only at the votes that really count. news.summary: Mitch McConnell returned to the Senate this week after a three-month absence.

news.title: Trump says Kennedy Center could be 'ripped down' if he doesn't get 'recognition'
news.text:
President Donald Trump said on Wednesday the Kennedy Center could "close" or be "ripped down" if his administration doesn't receive recognition on the performing arts center as tensions over his name being removed mount.

"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down," the president told reporters on the tarmac in North Carolina.

Trump claimed that the Kennedy Center was a "mess" without his intervention and "has lost 10s of millions of dollars, even hundreds of millions of dollars," comparing it to New York's Carnegie Hall.

The president's comments come after a federal judge on Tuesday blocked the performing arts center's board from adding a tribute to Trump on the building or site. He responded by saying he wouldn't spend congressionally approved funding for the center's renovation unless the building also bears his name.

Congress last year appropriated $257 million for the renovation.

About an hour after the judge's ruling Tuesday, the board, which is controlled by Trump appointees, voted to close the center immediately for renovations, citing safety concerns after a piece of plaster from the ceiling of the grand foyer fell during a heavy rainstorm earlier this month.

On Tuesday, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, said Trump “threw a tantrum because he lost in court” when discussing the Kennedy Center meeting.

“He wasn't pleased with it. He was very explicit with his words, and I responded equally as explicit. He is in contempt of court for what he's doing now in trying to just simply go over and close the Kennedy Center and to have people leave the center,” Beatty told reporters on the House steps Tuesday night.

Beatty said “there was a heated debate” during the meeting.

On Wednesday, fencing was seen being installed around the main building's entrance.
news.summary: The president's comments come after a federal judge on Tuesday blocked the performing arts center's board from adding a tribute to Trump on the building or site.

news.title: Trump voices concerns over Canada-EU proposal
news.text:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed making Canada the European Union’s first associate member, a striking overture as US President Donald Trump’s threats drive Ottawa closer to Europe.

Speaking in Charlotte, North Carolina, Mr Trump suggested that allowing Canada to become an associate EU member could be a “hostile act” and threatened to respond to the proposed move by imposing more tariffs on the bloc.

Mr Trump conditioned his threat on the “intention” of European leaders, saying that: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”

He also suggested the US could cut off trade with Europe in certain areas.

Mr Trump called the prospect of Canada joining the EU “laughable” and called America’s neighbour a “terrible trade partner”.

Mr Trump’s tariffs and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have soured the relationship between the North American neighbours.

Canada is seeking to reduce its dependence on the United States, the destination for roughly 70% of its exports, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU.

In her annual State of the European Union address, Ms von der Leyen said Canada and the EU would build on their existing free trade agreement, known as CETA, with a broader “Alliance for the Future” aimed at creating “a common prosperity and economic security space”.

She cast that closer relationship as rooted not just in trade but in shared democratic values.

“Above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy,” Ms von der Leyen said to Mr Carney, who received a standing ovation at the European Parliament in Strasbourg. He is due to address the Parliament on Thursday.

A Canadian official familiar with the discussions told The Associated Press last week that Ottawa was exploring ties with the EU that could stop just short of membership.

The official said Canada would seek an arrangement allowing its citizens to live and work in Europe without visas as part of a broader strategic partnership.

Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said on Wednesday that Ottawa had discussed associate membership with European officials before Ms von der Leyen’s speech and “knew that that was something that was on the table”.

He said Canada had talked to the EU about an “Alliance for the Future”, while European officials had raised associate membership.

Mr Wilkinson said Canada is not seeking full EU membership because it would require surrendering some sovereignty. Instead, Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc in a way that strengthens Canadian sovereignty rather than diminishes it, he said.

Mr Carney’s office welcomed Ms von der Leyen’s proposal, saying Canada was deepening ties with the EU “to strengthen our sovereignty” and supported a move beyond CETA.

Ms Von der Leyen said the expanded partnership would cover advanced manufacturing, technology, defence production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cyber-security and economic security.

“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. “In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”

Because Canada joining the EU as an associate member would be a first, there is no rule book on how that would work or what it would mean in practice. It is unclear who would need to approve membership, and how long that could take.

Mr Wilkinson said Ottawa and Brussels are deliberately focusing first on the substance of the relationship rather than what to call it.

“Before you actually get to the point where you decide what you’re going to call something, you should actually know the shape,” he said.

He said the shape is likely to become clearer at the Canada-EU summit in October, when the two sides expect to make an announcement and may settle on how to describe it.

Currently, all steps towards EU membership must be approved unanimously by the 27 member countries.

The idea of associate membership has been floated in the past for Ukraine, or for post-Brexit Britain, but no concrete steps have been taken.

The relationship between Canada and the European Union has reached a point where the two sides need to move beyond rhetoric and start building something more substantive, said Tobias Cremer, a German member of the European Parliament.

“Now is the time to stop sending each other love letters and put meat on the bone,” said Mr Cremer, from the centre-left Social Democrats.

He argued that any new arrangement should be more ambitious than another trade or defence agreement, describing the goal as a more holistic strategic alliance between Canada and the EU.

Existing frameworks such as CETA could provide a foundation, Mr Cremer said, but should be used more fully and expanded. The case for closer ties, he said, is increasingly being driven by geopolitics as much as economics.
news.author: Rob Gillies

news.title: 'Juvenile': Trump aide rages that voters don't care about his name on things
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s dogged insistence to put his name on a memorial built to honor a different president appears more and more difficult to defend. One by one, even Trump’s own strategists and Republican allies are warning him to surrender what looks like a “juvenile” crusade.

Trump’s own strategist, David Urban, was no less judgmental while speaking with CNN’s Anderson Cooper Wednesday night.

“Right. There's no way to defend the Kennedy Center piece or some of these other moves,” said Urban, who worked for Trump in his first term. “The president needs to pivot from what he's doing and get back to talking about what people around the kitchen table care about. I guarantee you, nobody in Beaver County, Pennsylvania, gives one hoot about the Kennedy Center, either way.”

“They care about gas prices. They care about what that $20 bill in their pocket does for them when they go to the grocery store, or when they go to the pump,” Urban continued. “And the president needs to tell them what he's going to do to make their life better and make that $20 go a little bit further.”

Urban found himself in unfamiliar territory: agreeing with Democratic Strategist Meghan Hays.

“You heard the president say that if the Trump administration doesn't get recognition for the Kennedy Center it’s going to end up being ripped down. Given all the other problems he's facing, does it make any sense to you that he is still fighting this?” Cooper asked Hays.

“No, his priorities are completely misaligned, but I think it's because he knows that he's made some really dumb mistakes when it comes to the economy with the Iran war and tariffs. And he doesn't know how to pivot out of it. So, he's being focused on all these vanity projects,” said Hays. “But what David said: the American people don't care about that. They care about their gas prices and their cost of groceries and how much they're paying for health care and child care. They could care less if their reflecting pool has water in it, or if there's a ballroom at the White House, or if the Kennedy center has his name on it. They literally just want some relief.”

Democratic strategist David Axelrod disagreed with Hays’ argument that Trump’s focus on the wrong priorities is a “pivot.”

“I disagree with Meghan a little. I don't think he's talking about those things to pivot away from the economy. He's interested in vanity projects because it may be because of vanity,” said Axelrod. “… [H]e wants to put his name on things. He can legitimately put his name on the highest diesel prices in history, because he does own that.”

news.title: How Trump’s war on EVs derailed America’s auto-factory revival
news.text: LORDSTOWN, Ohio - On a Friday afternoon in May, three men sat chatting on folding chairs inside Lordstown’s local United Auto Workers hall. Normally, they’d be on their shift at the massive battery plant a few miles away. But they’d been out of work all year.The factory — owned by General Motors and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution — announced last fall that work would stop in January because of slow electric-vehicle sales. Their joint venture, Ultium Cells, indefinitely let go about 480 employees, and told the remaining 850 factory workers they wouldn’t be needed for many months.That announcement came a few weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans killed a $7,500 tax credit that was intended to jumpstart consumer demand for electric cars, sending U.S. EV sales tumbling. The layoffs were a sobering letdown after the burst of optimism when the factory opened four years ago, said Steve Baier, one of the workers passing time inside the union hall.
news.summary: Since Trump returned to office, an array of automotive, environmental, trade and immigration policies has undermined factory projects and employment.

news.title: US Fed Raises Key Rate for First Time in 3 Years
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - The US Federal Reserve (Fed) on Wednesday raised interest rates by 25 basis points in an attempt to tackle stubbornly high inflation in the world's largest economy.This move is sure to anger President Donald Trump, who has called for lower rates and who recently nominated Kevin Warsh to the post of Federal Reserve Chair."Our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long," Warsh told a press conference.Warsh has served as Fed Chair since May and during his confirmation process, he had assured Congress that central bank policymakers would "have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation." "Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the committee's 2% goal," Warsh added.The increase boosts the Fed's target rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%.Trump had promised to lower prices in his 2024 election campaign, but things turned out differently after his inauguration. The US now faces the combined impact of Trump's global import tariffs, an energy shock following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom.After the announcement of the rate increase, Trump said US interest rates should ‌be 1% or lower and that the rates should be cut fast."I ... talked to Kevin," Trump said. "And I said you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They're very political. They're doing the wrong thing."Fed plans to 'stay in our lane'Since his appointment to the job, speculation circulated around which direction Warsh would take the Fed, as Trump has pressured the institution to follow his lead.But on Wednesday, Warsh joined the unanimous decision to raise interest rates, saying it had been made independent of what the market may be doing."We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation," he said. "I'll observe market prices and see what they have to say. But today was our decision.""Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane," Warsh said. "We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too. That's how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them."Borrowers will feel some impactThe raise in interest rates will affect those who borrow money to make large purchases, such as a home, car or large appliance. The new rate will also raise monthly payments and costs for those who are already paying interest on credit card debt.Currently, household debt payments are relatively low overall as a percentage of after-tax income. So many households will not feel the burden on borrowing in the short term. But the move could be good for those who are saving, as interest rates on savings accounts and certificates of deposit will rise.Read: JCI Falls as Investors Await US Fed Rate DecisionClick here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News
news.summary: The US Federal Reserve raised interest rates by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4% as inflation remains elevated

news.title: Federal Conservatives raise affordability, spectre of EU taxation ahead of B.C. caucus retreat
news.text:
A pitch for affordability was at the centre of the Conservative Party of Canada message ahead of the party’s caucus retreat in Penticton.

A brief press conference by Deputy Leader Melissa Lantsman on Sept. 16 was followed by an address by Party Leader Pierre Poilievre. 

Lantsman’s portion was focused on responding to recent reports that Prime Minister Mark Carney had approached the European Union about Canada becoming an association member, news that was first shared by the Wall Street Journal and the European Parliament and not the federal government. 

“None of this has been discussed here, with media, or with Parliament, or with Canadians and I think they need the straight goods with this,” said Lantsman. 

Carney’s office released a statement Wednesday morning about his meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, adding that he welcomed her proposal for Canada and the EU to move beyond the Canada-EU Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement “to a far stronger, more ambitious alliance in the future.”

Poilievre’s address was focused on the importance of finding ways to make life more affordable for Canadians, with a brief aside to state that he and the party would not support any associate membership that brought in any additional EU taxes or open border policy. 

The address opened by praising the Okanagan and recognizing the recent hardships following the latest wildfire season. 

“We Albertans love this province and our neighboring Okanagan, and we are all inspired by the firefighters, the first responders, the small businesses, the charities, the local agencies who’ve been fighting the fires and taking care of our beloved people,” said Poilievre. “All of Canada needs to learn from the resilience, the hardiness, and the determination of the people of Okanagan who’ve had a very difficult and smoky summer.”

The majority of the address to the caucus was on the role of the Opposition, not to criticize the government while abroad, but to push back and offer alternatives while at home. 

“People want our government to succeed in the face of the unfair tariffs and trolling from President (Donald) Trump and his administration, and we as Conservatives know about this, because as the party of confederation we always put Canadians above all else,” said Poilievre. 

He spoke to the conversations he had been having while Parliament was in recess, including with loggers in B.C., small business owners, and other Canadians currently struggling. 

Poilievre said the Canadian promise of working hard, following the rules and loving the country being enough to be rewarded with affordability and a safe neighbourhood was not being upheld, and that all of the summits and speeches since the last election had not translated into tangible improvements. 

He said the party, after scouring the last budget, claims to have found $150 billion in savings. 

Red tape, both at the provincial, municipal, and federal level was once again cited as being largely responsible. He used the difficulties in selling alcohol across provincial borders as one example of the barriers that were still in place. 

He also promised savings by outright eliminating taxes on multiple things, such as home building, fuel, and GST for vehicles made in Canada, as well as the capital gains tax for people investing in Canada. 

“If the U.S. wants to raise costs on its businesses through tariffs, we must respond by lowering them on ours,” said Poilievre. 

The remainder of the address reiterated previous Conservative positions, namely seeking to tighten up bail, repeal the gun-buyback, to reduce immigration and to move forward with projects awaiting approval for permits.
news.summary: Deputy Leader Melissa Lantsman said the party is strong and united

news.title: Trump threatens EU over ‘hostile’ Canada association plan
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump threatened on Wednesday to cut trade with the European Union after the bloc proposed to make Canada its first ever associate member.

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen raised the prospect a day before Canadian leader Mark Carney was due to address the European Parliament.

Her pitch comes as both Canada and the European Union seek to pivot away from an aggressive United States under Trump’s leadership.

“I think it’s laughable,” Trump told reporters when asked about the plan.

“If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things.”

He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility.”

Von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defense and energy to Carney, who became the first non-European head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” speech.

The German told the European Parliament in Strasbourg that, as democracies face a “fracture in the international rules-based system,” Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together.

“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen told the Canadian premier, drawing a standing ovation in the chamber.

A broader alliance

Carney has been pursuing closer ties with the European Union as Canada gets drawn ever deeper into a trade war with the United States.

He is set to address the parliament on Thursday, with his visit meant to act as a catalyst ahead of an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next month.

Von der Leyen said it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader “alliance for the future” and “bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”

“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defense industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said.

She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security as other fields of cooperation.

“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said.

But both the EU and Canada have been buffeted by tariffs and territorial threats from the US and competition from China.

“In a more dangerous and divided world, Canada is forging stronger relationships with trusted partners,” Carney’s office said in a statement.

What’s in a name?

While EU treaties do not envision the possibility of becoming an “associate member,” the idea was first floated by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz this year for Ukraine.

Under that plan, which met a cold reception from a country pushing for full membership, Ukraine would have been allowed to attend the bloc’s summits and have a representative in the European Commission.

It would have also benefited from parts of the EU budget, but without full voting rights.

“We don’t really know yet what it means,” said Tobias Cremer, a center-left European lawmaker from Germany and the main sponsor of a resolution urging stronger EU-Canada cooperation, after von der Leyen’s “associate membership” pitch.

Under EU rules, member states have to approve any form of partnership with a third country and it was unclear how much support von der Leyen’s proposal would receive from capitals.

Brussels and Ottawa already enjoy a considerable level of cooperation.

The CETA free-trade agreement that abolished almost all tariffs has been credited with boosting trade in goods and services by more than 80 percent since 2016.

And this year Canada became the first non-EU country to join a flagship defense loan program.

Carney later flew to Britain for his first meeting with new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

They attended a football match between Everton and Wolverhampton together before Carney’s return to Strasbourg for his Thursday speech.

news.title: Congress passes sweeping US sanctions bill targeting Russia
news.text:
The United States House of Representatives has passed a bipartisan sanctions bill targeting Russia over its continued war in Ukraine.

Lawmakers on Wednesday voted to send the sweeping legislation, championed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, to US President Donald Trump’s desk, ending more than a year of delays and obstacles. The final vote was 262 to 159. It had already passed in the US Senate.

The much-anticipated bill would give the president new abilities to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries, like China and India, that import energy supplies from Russia, allowing Washington to further restrict funds sent to Moscow. The measure would also impose sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has been pushing for the bill’s passage and made a direct appeal to senators shortly before they passed it last month.

Fifty-eight Democrats bucked their party’s leadership and joined with a majority of Republicans to pass it.

The Democratic Party has overwhelmingly supported Ukraine in the war. However, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries opposed the bill, citing new tariff authorities given to the White House that could be used to exploit US allies.

“The manner in which this bill has been written doesn’t require the president of the United States to impose sanctions on Russia,” Jeffries said on the House floor Wednesday. “In fact, there are so many loopholes written into the bill, I believe, that it’s very unlikely that the sanctions relief contemplated in the legislation will ever see the light of day.”

The bill marks the first time in more than two years the US Congress has passed legislation supporting Ukraine. Graham, after whom the bill was named following his sudden death in July, had helped negotiate Trump’s support for it.

House Speaker Mike Johnson heralded the bill’s passage, saying it places “maximum pressure on … the Russian war machine”, including the country’s President Vladimir Putin.

“For too long, Putin has bankrolled this devastating war with money and resources from countries willing to look the other way, and today, that ends,” Johnson said in a post on social media. “This bill sends a powerful message of American unity and gives the Administration every tool in the toolbox to help bring this war to a just end, and we are proud to send it to the President’s desk.”

After the vote, a group of Republicans and Democrats from the House and Senate celebrated the vote at a rare bipartisan news conference.

Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, who wrote the bill with Graham, said he hopes the sanctions will help force Putin to the negotiating table and end the war.

“To Vladimir Putin – we have your number,” Blumenthal said. “And to Ukraine – you are not alone.”

Trump is expected to sign the bill into law.

news.title: House passes Russia and Iran sanctions bill championed by Sen. Lindsey Graham
news.text:
The House passed a Russia and Iran sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham Wednesday night -- sending the measure to President Donald Trump's desk for his signature.

The final tally was 262-159.

Seven Republicans -- Reps. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Andy Harris of Maryland, Ralph Norman of South Carolina, Keith Self of Texas, Tom McClintock of California, Chip Roy of Texas and Warren Davidson of Ohio -- voted against the measure.

The bill's passage comes about two months after Graham's sudden death.

The package would impose primary and secondary sanctions on Russia and other countries that support Russia in its invasion of Ukraine. The sanctions target Russian political officials and oligarchs, banks and financial institutions, and the Russian shadow fleet, according to the bill.

The legislation also allows for the president to impose tariffs but limits the scope of those tariffs to the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas and the top five countries that aid Russia's energy sanctions evasion.

It also includes a provision to prevent a lapse in sanction authority that restricts funding for Iran's energy and weapons sectors.

In a statement on social media, Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who was appointed to fill her late brother's Senate seat and is now running for a full term, celebrate the measure's passage.

"Today is a monumental day for peace," she wrote in the post on X. "This legislation was deeply important to my brother, Lindsey, and I'm grateful that it achieved such a wide coalition of support on the House floor. I am committed to achieving a peaceful resolution to the war in Ukraine, and I'm confident that this legislation will pave the way."

The vote split Democrats -- 58 voted in favor while 152 voted against.

Top House Democratic leaders including Leader Hakeem Jeffries explained why they voted against the sanctions bill, saying it “gives extraordinary power to Donald Trump.”

“It allows him to waive the sanctions contained in the bill, while giving him new, expansive tariff authority to continue his failed global trade war that is causing costs to skyrocket for working families across America," they said. "Sadly, the White House is willing to risk Ukrainian lives and American livelihoods instead of working to actually hold this rogue Russian regime accountable for its illegal war."

Earlier this week, several Democrats, including Reps. Gregory Meeks, Richard Neal and Don Beyer, voiced concerns with the bill but expressed their staunch support for Ukraine.

The Senate approved the measure last month with overwhelming bipartisan support by a vote of 86-11.
news.summary: The House passed a Russia and Iran sanctions bill championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham Wednesday night.

news.title: Trump Threatens Trade Measures Against Europe if Canada’s Potential EU Associate Membership Done as a ‘Hostile Act’
news.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump says that if Canada joins the European Union as a proposed associate member intended as a “hostile act” against the United States, he may impose tariffs on Europe or halt trade with the bloc.

Trump was asked about European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal for Canada to become an associate member by reporters Sept. 16 in Charlotte, N.C., while on the way to a campaign rally in support of Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley.

“I think it’s laughable,” Trump said, while calling Canada a “terrible trade partner.” He added that if the intention behind the initiative is a “hostile act,” he would impose consequences.

“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump said adding that he may even fully cut off trade with the bloc in some areas.

Earlier on Sept. 16, Trump signed an order to enact an earlier commitment to remove Canadian goods from certain U.S. federal procurement contracts.

Trump’s reaction comes after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she would like to create a new pathway for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member” during her Sept. 16 state of the union address in Strasbourg, France, which Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney attended.

Von der Leyen said that the proposed associate member status could include closer collaboration in numerous areas including trade, defence, artificial intelligence, and technology.

Carney hasn’t directly rejected becoming an “associate member” of the bloc, but has said his country wouldn’t become a “member,” and that it’s seeking a “unique alliance.”

Carney’s office said Sept. 16 that he “welcomed” von der Leyen’s proposal and supported moving beyond trade agreements to a closer relationship.

Canadian Ambassador to the EU Jonathan Wilkinson confirmed that an associate membership for Canada has been discussed by both sides.

Trump’s comments come in the midst of an ongoing trade dispute between Washington and Ottawa.

Talks between the two sides broke down Aug. 21 after Ottawa walked away from trade negotiations, with both sides blaming the other for last-minute changes in demand.

While criticizing Canada’s trade practices, Trump said on Sept. 12 that a deal between the two countries could be reached “fairly soon.” Carney said this week that he welcomes that, adding that his government is “ready to sit down and negotiate” with Washington.

news.title: Trump believes Iran seeks deal with US but not yet ready for it
news.text:
WASHINGTON, September 17. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump believes that Iran is seeking to reach a deal with the United States but is not yet ready for it.

"They call: ‘We want to make a deal. We want to make it,’" Trump added. "They're not ready yet. I don't think, but we could have a deal any time we want."

He reiterated his forecast that the conflict will end after the midterm elections to the US Congress due in November, adding that he also sees a possibility of an earlier solution.

The US and Israel began a war with Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, on the night of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached regarding the Strait of Hormuz, through which approximately 25% of global oil trade and about 20% of liquefied natural gas (LNG) trade pass. Subsequently, the US administration effectively signaled an end to the use of large-scale military force against Iran, shifting toward an attempt to economically strangle the country through sanctions.
